source_evidence.anchor: opening rectangular matrix setting and column notation
source_evidence.observation: The standing setting is A in R^{m×n}, m >= n, rank(A)=n. The paper writes A=(a_1,...,a_n), Q=(q_1,...,q_n), and R=(r_jk); Q is m×n and R is n×n.

Algorithm 2 is the CGS-P variant. It constructs Q_k=[Q_{k-1},q_k] and the leading upper-triangular R_k, ending with Q=Q_n and R=R_n. The surrounding model assumes IEEE arithmetic, machine unit ε_M, normalized-range results, and first-order omission of O(ε_M^2).

source_evidence.anchor: definitions immediately before Theorem 1 and equations (3)-(8)
source_evidence.observation: A_k is explicitly the first k columns of A, κ_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^{-1}||_2, and Theorem 1 assumes c_4(m,k)ε_Mκ_2(R_k)^2<1 for every k. For k=1,...,n it defines the factorization residual ΔA_k by Q_kR_k-A_k=ΔA_k and the Gram residual E_k by R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k=E_k, with first-order norm bounds.

source_evidence.anchor: Lemma 2 proof paragraph beginning 'Using (3), we conclude that R is nonsingular'
source_evidence.observation: The proof invokes condition (3) to conclude that R is nonsingular and that r_kk>0 for every k; hence the leading triangular factors used later have ordinary inverses.

source_evidence.anchor: proof of Theorem 1, paragraph beginning 'If we let ΔA_k'
source_evidence.observation: The proof explicitly sets ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k, confirming that ΔA_k is the exact analytical factorization residual, not a separately computed algorithm output.

source_evidence.anchor: proof of equation (5), display beginning 'E_k = R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k'
source_evidence.observation: The proof explicitly sets E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k and displays it as a k×k block matrix, confirming the residual's sign and dimensions.

source_evidence.anchor: unnumbered two-line displayed identity beginning 'I-Q_k^T Q_k'
source_evidence.observation: Immediately after Q_k=(A_k+ΔA_k)R_k^{-1}, the paper gives an exact two-line equality expressing I-Q_k^TQ_k first through R_k^TR_k-(A_k+ΔA_k)^T(A_k+ΔA_k), and then through E_k, the two cross terms, and the quadratic residual term.

binders: Inherited binder: A is a real m×n matrix with m >= n and rank(A)=n. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 300), anchor: opening rectangular matrix setting and column notation.]
Explicit theorem binder: ε_M is the machine unit for the floating-point execution of Algorithm 2. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 opening assumption.]

Quantifier order: first assume condition (3) for every prefix k; then the theorem's conclusions, including the identity used in proving (7), apply for each k=1,...,n. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 and equation (3).]

For fixed k, A_k and Q_k are m×k, while R_k is k×k; ΔA_k is m×k and E_k is k×k. The A_k dimension is explicit, and the remaining dimensions follow from the column-prefix and block constructions. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2 block construction; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: A_k definition and equations (4)-(5).]
hypotheses: Inherited paper setting: A has full column rank and m >= n. Theorem 1 does not restate this opening assumption. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 300), anchor: opening rectangular matrix setting; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1.]

The matrices Q_k and R_k are computed prefixes produced by Algorithm 2, CGS-P, in floating-point arithmetic with machine unit ε_M. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 opening assumption.]

For every k, c_4(m,k)ε_Mκ_2(R_k)^2<1. The proof uses this restriction to obtain nonsingularity and positive diagonal entries. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (3) and post-theorem nonsingularity sentence; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 307), anchor: consequence of condition (3).]

For the selected algebraic identity itself, the operative hypotheses are the exact residual definitions and availability of R_k^{-1}; the floating-point bounds and rounding equations do not occur in the displayed equality. [PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: exact definition of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: exact definition of E_k; PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
conclusions: From ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k and invertibility of R_k, Q_k=(A_k+ΔA_k)R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: display immediately preceding the selected identity.]

First line of the selected identity: I_k-Q_k^TQ_k = R_k^{-T}(R_k^TR_k-(A_k+ΔA_k)^T(A_k+ΔA_k))R_k^{-1}. The paper prints an unsubscripted I; conformability makes it I_k. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: first line of the unnumbered identity.]

Second line of the selected identity: I_k-Q_k^TQ_k = R_k^{-T}(E_k-A_k^TΔA_k-(ΔA_k)^TA_k-(ΔA_k)^T(ΔA_k))R_k^{-1}. All three subtracted residual contributions, including the quadratic term, are present. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: second line of the unnumbered identity.]
definitions_and_conventions: A_k consists of the first k columns of A; Algorithm 2 constructs Q_k by adjoining q_k and R_k as the corresponding leading k×k upper-triangular factor. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2 block construction; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: definition of A_k.]
ΔA_k is defined with sign ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k. [PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: paragraph 'If we let ΔA_k'.]
E_k is defined with sign E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k. [PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: display defining E_k.]
κ_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^{-1}||_2. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: definition immediately before Theorem 1.]
R_k^{-T} denotes the transpose of R_k^{-1}; the selected display uses ordinary inverse and inverse-transpose notation. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
The unsubscripted identity matrix in the paper's display has size k×k because Q_k^TQ_k and every middle residual expression are k×k. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
implicit_context: The selected identity is an intermediate exact calculation in the proof of Theorem 1's orthogonality-defect bound (7), and the proof explicitly says it is using results (4) and (5). [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: paragraphs 'To prove (6)-(8)' and 'To get (7)'.]

Q_k and R_k denote computed floating-point outputs, whereas ΔA_k and E_k are exact analytical residual matrices defined from those outputs and A_k. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: computed matrices and equations (4)-(5); PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: definition of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: definition of E_k.]

The opening exact-arithmetic statement Q^TQ=I_n describes the ideal factorization; the selected expression measures the actual orthogonality defect of computed Q_k. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 300), anchor: exact factorization (1); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]

From the upper-triangular prefix construction and the proof's conclusion that every r_kk is positive, each R_k used in the identity is nonsingular. This prefix-level conclusion is inferred from the displayed construction and proof. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2 block construction; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 307), anchor: r_kk>0 for all k.]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The theorem and selected proof concern Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like classical Gram-Schmidt variant CGS-P. For k>=2 it uses s_k=Q_{k-1}^Ta_k, v_k=a_k-Q_{k-1}s_k, ψ_k=||a_k||_2, φ_k=||s_k||_2, r_kk=(ψ_k-φ_k)^{1/2}(ψ_k+φ_k)^{1/2}, and q_k=v_k/r_kk. This is explicitly distinct from Algorithm 1, CGS-S, which uses r_kk=||v_k||_2. Algebraically the selected equality follows from residual definitions and invertibility, but its paper-level provenance is CGS-P. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 300), anchor: Algorithm 1 and transition to CGS-P; PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 opening assumption.]
numerical_model: The standing model assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic and states fl(x+y)=(x+y)(1+δ), |δ|<=ε_M, for results in the normalized range. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2.]

The paper adopts (1+ε_M)^{p(n)}=1+p(n)ε_M+O(ε_M^2) for modest p(n), treating the O(ε_M^2) contribution as insignificant. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: linear approximation following the IEEE model.]
Theorem 1 concerns computed Q_k and R_k and states its bounds to within O(ε_M^2). [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 before equations (4)-(8).]

No rounding operator, ε_M, or approximate-equality symbol appears in the selected two-line identity. It is exact real-matrix algebra applied to the computed matrices and exact residual definitions; the numerical model is inherited context rather than an algebraic premise of the equality. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
error_notions: ΔA_k is the factorization or backward residual Q_kR_k-A_k. Theorem 1 bounds ||ΔA_k||_2 by c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2ε_M to first order. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (4); PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: exact residual definition.]

E_k is the Gram-matrix residual R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k. Theorem 1 bounds ||E_k||_2 by c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2ε_M to first order. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (5); PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: exact residual definition.]

I_k-Q_k^TQ_k is the orthogonality defect. The selected identity expresses it exactly in terms of E_k, the two transpose-related cross terms, and the quadratic factorization-residual term. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (7); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]

ΔA_k and E_k are analysis variables, not quantities listed as outputs of Algorithm 2. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2 outputs Q and R; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: introduction of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: introduction of E_k.]
norms: The paper uses ||·||_2 for vectors and matrices and defines κ_2 through this norm. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 300), anchor: algorithmic vector norms; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: κ_2 definition and residual bounds.]

For matrices, the intended norm is the spectral/operator 2-norm; this is supported by the paper's equality ||R_k||_2^2=||R_k^TR_k||_2. The cited pages do not separately define the norm in words. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: opening calculation in the proof of (6).]

The selected equality itself is a matrix identity and contains no norm. The immediately following argument applies ||·||_2 to derive the orthogonality bound. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity and following 'Thus' inequality.]
constants_and_indexing: The prefix index is k=1,...,n. Algorithm 2 has a base step k=1 and a loop k=2,...,n; there is no shifted index in the selected identity. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 quantifier.]
The preceding definitions give c_1(m,1)=1 and c_1(m,k)=2√(2mk)+2√k for k=2,...,n. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (2).]
They give c_2(m,1)=m+2 and c_2(m,k)=3.5mk^2-1.5mk+16k for k=2,...,n, together with c_3(m,k)=0.5c_2(m,k) and c_4(m,k)=c_2(m,k)+2c_1(m,k). [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (2).]

Condition (3) is c_4(m,k)ε_Mκ_2(R_k)^2<1 for every prefix k. No c_i constant appears in the selected exact identity itself. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: equation (3); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
higher_order_terms: Theorem 1 places a blanket qualification 'to within terms of O(ε_M^2)' on equations (4)-(8) and their bounds. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: sentence immediately before equations (4)-(8).]

The selected identity has no omitted or big-O term. In particular, -(ΔA_k)^T(ΔA_k) is explicitly retained rather than discarded as second order. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: second line of the selected identity.]
Only after the exact identity does the norm estimate absorb higher-order contributions into O(ε_M^2). [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: norm inequalities following 'Thus'.]
exceptional_values: The stated floating-point relation is restricted to results in the normalized range. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: IEEE floating-point paragraph.]

Under condition (3), the proof concludes that R is nonsingular, every r_kk is positive, and Algorithm 2 has ψ_k>φ_k; these facts make the divisions, square roots, and inverses used in the theorem available. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 307), anchor: consequence of condition (3).]

The cited model gives no explicit handling rule for overflow, underflow, subnormal values, NaNs, or infinities; the normalized-range qualification is the only stated exceptional-value restriction in this context. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: floating-point model following Algorithm 2.]

undebatable_constraints: The source-level algorithm is Algorithm 2 (CGS-P), not Algorithm 1 (CGS-S). [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1 opening assumption.]

The identity is prefixwise for k=1,...,n, with A_k,Q_k,ΔA_k rectangular m×k and R_k,E_k,I_k square k×k. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: prefix block construction; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: A_k definition and equations (4)-(5); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]

The residual signs are ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k and E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k. Reversing either sign changes the source identity. [PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: definition of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: definition of E_k.]

Both equality stages must be preserved: the unexpanded congruence involving R_k^TR_k-(A_k+ΔA_k)^T(A_k+ΔA_k), and its expansion through E_k. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: two-line selected identity.]

The expanded middle expression contains exactly E_k-A_k^TΔA_k-(ΔA_k)^TA_k-(ΔA_k)^T(ΔA_k), with all three minus signs and the quadratic term present. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: second line of the selected identity.]
Ordinary R_k^{-1} and R_k^{-T} are required; no pseudoinverse occurs in the selected identity. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: Q_k relation and selected identity.]

The selected identity is exact and contains no ε_M, inequality, norm, or O(ε_M^2) remainder, even though it is embedded in a floating-point error analysis. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity and following norm estimate.]
The paper prints I without a subscript, but its only conformable interpretation in the identity is the k×k identity I_k. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]

ambiguities.issue: The displayed identity writes I rather than I_k. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
ambiguities.evidence: Q_k is an m×k prefix, so Q_k^TQ_k is k×k, and the residual expression between R_k^{-T} and R_k^{-1} is also k×k. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Q_k and R_k block construction; PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
ambiguities.impact: A formal statement must instantiate I as the k×k identity; treating it as I_n or I_m is dimensionally incompatible. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]

ambiguities.issue: The theorem defines κ_2(R_k) using R_k^{-1} before saying that restriction (3) assures nonsingularity. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: κ_2 definition, condition (3), and post-theorem nonsingularity sentence.]
ambiguities.evidence: The later proof resolves the intended regime by invoking (3) to conclude that R is nonsingular and r_kk>0 for every k. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 307), anchor: consequence of condition (3).]
ambiguities.impact: The selected identity must be read only for invertible R_k; the paper supplies no singular-case convention or replacement by a generalized inverse. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: occurrences of R_k^{-1} and R_k^{-T}.]

ambiguities.issue: The cited pages use matrix ||·||_2 without a standalone verbal definition. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: κ_2 and theorem bounds.]
ambiguities.evidence: The equality ||R_k||_2^2=||R_k^TR_k||_2 on printed page 312 identifies the intended matrix norm as the spectral/operator 2-norm. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: opening calculation in the proof of (6).]
ambiguities.impact: A translation should use the spectral/operator matrix 2-norm for the surrounding bounds, while recognizing that the selected equality itself is norm-free. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity and following norm estimate.]

ambiguities.issue: Theorem 1's phrase 'to within terms of O(ε_M^2)' grammatically precedes equations (4)-(8), which could make the status of the residual equalities appear approximate. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: sentence before equations (4)-(8).]
ambiguities.evidence: The proof later defines ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k and E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k exactly, and the selected identity retains the full quadratic residual term with no O notation. [PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: definition of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: definition of E_k; PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity.]
ambiguities.impact: The residual norm estimates are first-order, but the selected matrix identity is exact; adding an O term to it or deleting (ΔA_k)^T(ΔA_k) would not match the displayed source. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity and subsequent bound.]

contract_plain_english: In the paper's CGS-P setting, fix any prefix k=1,...,n and define the exact residuals ΔA_k=Q_kR_k-A_k and E_k=R_k^TR_k-A_k^TA_k. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 309), anchor: definition of ΔA_k; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 310), anchor: definition of E_k.] When R_k is invertible, Q_k=(A_k+ΔA_k)R_k^{-1}, and the k×k orthogonality defect equals R_k^{-T}(R_k^TR_k-(A_k+ΔA_k)^T(A_k+ΔA_k))R_k^{-1}, which in turn equals R_k^{-T}(E_k-A_k^TΔA_k-(ΔA_k)^TA_k-(ΔA_k)^T(ΔA_k))R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: preceding Q_k relation and unnumbered two-line identity.] This is an exact algebraic identity for the computed factors and analytical residuals; the IEEE model, condition-number restriction, first-order bounds, and O(ε_M^2) omissions belong to the surrounding theorem and subsequent inequality, not to the equality itself. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 301), anchor: floating-point model; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 302), anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 14 (printed p. 312), anchor: selected identity and following norm estimate.]
